title: SLO-and-cost-signal-positioning-against-cloud-hyperscalers
content:
Executive summary:

This note crystallizes a distinct go-to-market angle vs. hyperscaler managed endpoints (AWS SageMaker/Bedrock-ish flows, GCP Vertex, Azure Managed/OpenAI): lead with SLO-first operational signals + unit cost predictability. Instead of a generic feature vs. feature spreadsheet, field teams should anchor conversations on predictable business outcomes: percent of requests meeting latency SLOs, token-level cost variance, and graceful degradation guarantees when capacity is constrained.

Why this matters to buyers:
- Engineering and platform buyers are tired of surprise bills and opaque cost amplification when load or sequence length changes.
- Product teams need confidence that user-facing latency SLOs (p95/p99) hold across peak traffic and model upgrades.
- Security/compliance buyers need clear isolation and routing guarantees for regulated workloads that hyperscalers only partly solve with complicated network constructs.

Buyer personas and top questions:
- Platform/Infra Lead: "How can I guarantee latency for our chat feature during peak events without overprovisioning?"
- ML/Model Ops Lead: "If I swap to a quantized variant or a 7B vs 70B model, what changes for cost and latency — and how do we test that safely?"
- Product Manager (customer-facing): "What happens to UX if a region loses capacity — do we fail closed or degrade with a known policy?"

Competitor shorthand (what they say vs. our counter):
- AWS-managed endpoints (SageMaker/Bedrock flows): 
  - Competitor claim: "Enterprise integrations, pay-as-you-go, huge model catalog and regional footprint."
  - How to respond: Acknowledge breadth, then press on operational transfer cost: ask how they measure token-level price variance and p99 tail across model variants. Highlight Redwood's routing and automatic model-fallback policies that preserve SLOs while reducing overprovisioning.
- GCP Vertex AI: 
  - Competitor claim: "Tight cloud integration and familiar billing/permissions."
  - How to respond: Validate the convenience story, then differentiate on predictable unit economics for production inference: Redwood surfaces token/route-level cost and latency telemetry per deployment and provides batching/cache suggestions tuned per workload.
- Azure / Azure OpenAI managed endpoints: 
  - Competitor claim: "First-class enterprise support and Microsoft ecosystem integrations."
  - How to respond: Surface Redwood's private deployment options (VPC/on-prem) with enterprise SLAs that include model-variant rollouts and automatic guarded fallbacks, plus per-route observability tailored to SLOs.

Primary win themes (short plays):
1) SLO-observability first: Show a one-pager with p50/p95/p99 latency and token-cost splits by route and model. This is a high-leverage demo for platform buyers.
2) Predictable unit economics: Use Redwood Optimize recommendations to produce a recommended config that lowers per-token cost by X% with constrained latency delta. Frame as "what we will guarantee in the pilot."
3) Graceful degradation and fallback guarantees: Sell the ability to define policy-level fallbacks (region/model/capacity tier) that maintain response correctness and bounded latency.
4) Private and isolated flow: For regulated buyers, lead with Private deployment options, KMS/HSM support, and audit logging for inference traces.

Proof points and artifacts to show in sell cycles:
- Token-level billing breakdown demo (console screenshot + anonymized customer example)
- A/B rollout example where a model upgrade was rolled out to 10% and automatically rolled back on eval regression
- Incident timeline where automatic fallback preserved p99 latency during a GPU pool failure
- Quantified case study: "Customer X reduced 99th percentile latency by 30% and cut inference spend by 22% by adopting Redwood batching + KV caching"

Objections and rebuttals (concise):
- "Hyperscalers already give us managed endpoints and lower ops burden." 
  - Rebuttal: "They do — but their economics can be hidden and tail latency tunables are limited. For production SLA-backed products, the ability to route, cache, and failover deterministically matters more than single-call manageability."
- "We like the ecosystem integrations (IAM, logging, billing)."
  - Rebuttal: "Redwood supports the same integrations for hosted and private deployments; plus we provide per-route tracing and developer controls that reduce mean time to resolve model regressions."
- "We can self-host if we care about cost and control."
  - Rebuttal: "If you already have infra expertise and want a turnkey runtime, Redwood gives you the predictable economics and rollouts without building KV cache, batching, and kernel selection tech from scratch."

Field playbook (how to run a pilot):
1) Quick 2-week pilot scope: instrument 1–3 critical routes (chat, search, rerank). Baseline token counts, p95/p99 latency, and request size distribution.
2) Run Redwood Optimize audit: provide quantization and batching recommendations + expected delta in cost and latency.
3) Configure SLOs and run canary (10% traffic) with automatic regression alerts and a rollback guard.
4) Present pilot results as a 1-slide before/after (p95/p99, cost per 1k tokens, error rate).

Suggested battle assets (create/update):
- One-pager SLO vs Cost quick-start (2 pages): template for sales engineers to print for customers.
- Demo script: "Live token billing breakdown + fallback demo" (5–7 minutes).
- Objection playbook card: top 3 hyperscaler claims and 1-line counters.

Quick sample talk tracks (short):
- Platform lead: "We’ll define p95/p99 SLOs for these routes, show you current variance, and then demonstrate a config that reduces your overprovision by X% while preserving p99 targets."
- ML lead: "We can test a 7B quantized variant as a canary — Redwood will route and fallback automatically if quality or latency regresses."

Email template for initial outreach (field):
Subject: Quick idea to stabilize latency and reduce inference cost for [Product]
Hi [Name],
We ran an SLO-first audit for a company similar to [company] and identified three levers that cut inference spend while keeping p99 latency stable: targeted batching, prefix/KV caching, and an automated failover policy that degrades gracefully during capacity events. Can we run a short pilot on a sample route?
Thanks,
[Asha]

Open questions / follow-ups for product:
- Exportable SLO report: build an export that shows per-route p50/p95/p99 with token cost broken down by model and time window.
- Field-configurable fallback templates: small library for common patterns (regional-first, model-size-fallback, capacity-tier-fallback).
- Pricing anchor: define a pilot pricing guarantee for 30-day pilots (cap on cost variance).

Notes to self (informal):
- Avoid getting into model architecture arguments in early convo. Keep it about outcomes (latency, cost, availability).
- Get engineering to add a canned demo scenario showing a holiday spike and automatic fallback preserving p99.

Appendix: short competitive signal map (one-liners)
- AWS: breadth, enterprise deals, billing complexity.
- GCP: deep cloud integration, SKU complexity.
- Azure: enterprise accounts + Microsoft bundling.
- Redwood: SLO-first ops, predictable unit economics, private deployment options, guided optimize recommendations.

End.
